worst_places.before: A token is an extension point: (a) in tests the config is supplied by a provider (`provideAppConfig({ apiUrl: '/api' })`), so tests do not depend on which stand the code was built for (chapter 13); (b) the value can be obtained at runtime — from `index.html`, from a server response, from an environment variable through `define` — so one artifact can be deployed to several stands with no rebuild.
worst_places.after: A token is an extension point, and that buys you two things. First, tests: the config comes from a provider, `provideAppConfig({ apiUrl: '/api' })`, so a test no longer depends on which environment the code was built for (chapter 13). Second, runtime: the value can arrive from `index.html`, from a server response, or from `define`. One build artifact then deploys to staging and to production without a rebuild.

patterns: The abbreviation debt is back-loaded onto the last chapters. Chapters 08-15 are where the infrastructure vocabulary arrives (CORS, XHR, XSS, SDK, LCP, CLS, CDN, CI, CSP, SSRF, SEO, SPA, RTL, CVA, a11y, e2e) and the course never opened a glossary — even DI, DOM, SSR and JSX, first used back in chapters 00-04, are unexpanded there too. Because a course is read in order, an unexplained acronym in chapter 12 or 15 has no earlier chapter to fall back on: the reader must leave the page. The two densest chapters (12: LCP+CLS+CDN+CI; 15: nine terms) are also the last two, i.e. the ones a reader reaches most tired. This is the single highest-value fix in the zone and it is mechanical.

The English version is systematically about twice the Russian long-sentence rate for identical content: RU runs 5-10% of sentences over 25 words, EN runs 19-24.5%. Two causes stack. First, the translation keeps every RU em-dash clause and then pays English's ~19% word tax on top, so a comfortable 45-word RU sentence becomes an unreadable 60-70-word EN one. Second, where the RU is plain the EN reaches for a vivid idiom a B1-B2 reader will not know: 'junk drawers', 'smeared across four folders', 'fertile ground for cycles', 'would be sabotage', 'in earnest', 'eyeballed optimizations', 'the flip side of coldness', 'battle-tested'. Chapters 14 and 15 are the worst, and en/15 carries a live Russianism — «стенд» rendered as 'stand' four times where English needs 'environment'.

The 'Ответы на edge cases' / 'Answers to the edge cases' block is the one place where the otherwise excellent pyramid inverts. Every ordinary section opens with the answer in plain words ('Ключевая идея:', 'Главная мысль:', 'Первая — http.get() без подписки'), which is why criterion C scores 4.5 across the zone. But nearly every 50-word-plus sentence in all sixteen files lives inside these answer bullets and inside the 'Проверь себя' answers: they routinely open with a single sentence carrying three or four facts, listed (a)/(b)/(c), before any of them lands. The fix is uniform — lead each bullet with a one-line verdict, then the reasons as separate sentences.

Solution-walkthrough snippets are illustrative rather than runnable, and the two locales have drifted. Every chapter correctly states its input ('Вход: проект из главы 08'), so the course allowance on rubric E mostly holds — but the code references classes the course never shows (AuthStore, Notifications, TicketDto, TicketDraft, TICKETS, makeTicket, CurrentUser, adminMatchGuard), ch09's TicketForm calls an undeclared this.router, and ru/09 keeps unused RxJS imports that en/09 already removed. There is no cross-locale sync check: en/10 also moved 'What we add to the project' above 'React parallels' while ru/10 keeps it two sections later.

Wide ASCII tables and box diagrams open sections before any prose does. This is the zone's greatest strength for concept density (D averages 3.8 with almost no unbroken theory) but it fights the phone reader: several tables run 100-110 characters wide, so on a narrow screen the first thing after a heading is a horizontally-scrolling block whose meaning only arrives in the paragraph below it. Where a section leads with a table, a one-line lead sentence before the table would keep the pyramid intact at no cost to the diagram.
notes:
RxJS overlap (ch09 vs the rxjs topic): complements, does not duplicate or contradict. Ch09 scopes itself to the Angular seam (toSignal/toObservable/takeUntilDestroyed/rxResource/AsyncPipe) and defers the model; switchMap/concatMap/mergeMap/exhaustMap semantics, shareReplay-without-refCount and toPromise deprecation all match the topic. But it does NOT teach marble notation and draws no marble diagram — it names the term once and links out to rxjs.dev instead of to rxjs/03, which teaches the notation properly. Swap that link.
Ch13 (testing): yes, a reader could learn testing from it — what/where/why, TestBed, DI swapping, HttpTestingController, harnesses, guards, e2e, the Vitest/fakeAsync break and the whenStable-vs-detectChanges reasoning, with eight graded exercises. Gaps: describe/it/expect/beforeEach are assumed rather than introduced, RTL is never spelled out, and there is nothing on test design (what to assert, arrange-act-assert) beyond 'assert behaviour, not markup'.
Ch15 (capstone): it does review the course — the 'Капстоун: что получилось' section maps all 15 chapters onto Support Desk plus a senior-polish checklist — but only after ~40% of the chapter has introduced genuinely new material (build configs, SSR, hydration, prerender, static deploy, caching, sanitization contexts, CSP). It is 'one more chapter with a review appendix', not a review chapter, and the review is a bullet list with no exercise that re-tests earlier material.
